extracted.intended_audience: national banks and Federal savings associations; bank counsel; mortgage lenders; industry stakeholders and public commenters on OCC rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: A Federal Register notice of proposed rulemaking by the OCC to codify banks' authority to establish and maintain real estate lending escrow accounts, define 'escrow account,' clarify that escrow terms (investment, fees, compensation) are bank business judgments, and provide the procedural/regulatory analyses and instructions for submitting comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escrow account — definitional standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Escrow account means an account established in connection with a loan or extension of credit secured by a lien on interest in real estate in which the borrower places funds for the purpose of assuring payment of taxes, insurance premiums, or other charges with respect to the property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed as identical or substantially similar definitions in 12 CFR part 34 (national banks) and part 160 (Federal savings associations); anchors regulatory scope and applicability of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to establish and maintain escrow accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: National banks and Federal savings associations may establish or maintain escrow accounts in connection with real estate loans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed regulatory language (e.g., new §34.3(d) and §160.30(b)) expressly codifies longstanding powers and clarifies that such activity is within banks' lending powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank discretion over escrow account terms and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms and conditions of any such escrow account, including the investment of escrowed funds, fees assessed for the provision of such accounts, or whether and to what extent interest or other compensation is calculated and paid to customers whose funds are placed in the escrow account, are business decisions to be made by each bank in its discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OCC proposes to codify that investment strategy, fee assessment, and whether to pay interest/compensation are discretionary business judgments subject to safe-and-sound banking principles and applicable law; this discretion is presented as core to banks' mortgage lending powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: RESPA escrow-account statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: RESPA requires disclosures as to the nature and purposes of escrow accounts; mandates the provision of free annual escrow account statements; requires amounts in escrow accounts be paid timely as they become due and any funds remaining in such accounts after the loan is repaid be promptly returned to the borrower; and establishes proportional caps on the total amounts that may be collected from borrowers in escrow accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RESPA regulates disclosure, timing of payments, account statements, return of funds, and caps on escrow collections but does not dictate use of escrowed funds or require payment of compensation/interest by lenders; banks must comply with RESPA and Regulation X (12 CFR 1024) when administering escrow accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interagency Guidelines — loan administration procedures (escrow administration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each insured depository institution should establish loan administration procedures for its real estate portfolio that address 'escrow administration' along with other core aspects such as 'documentation,' 'loan closing and disbursement,' 'payment processing,' 'collateral administration,' 'loan payoffs,' 'collections and foreclosures,' 'claims processing,' and 'servicing and participation agreements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines outline topics banks should address; they provide structure but afford substantial flexibility in how institutions satisfy escrow administration responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escrow account administration operational practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Escrow account administration consists of (1) setting up the account, (2) crediting the account for tax and insurance funds received as part of the borrower's monthly mortgage payment, (3) making timely payments of the borrower's obligations, (4) analyzing the account balance in relation to anticipated payments annually, and (5) reporting the account balance to the borrower annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Servicers must closely monitor property taxing authorities and insurance contracts to ensure escrow calculations are accurate and policies have not lapsed; must ensure compliance with RESPA (12 U.S.C. 2609) and Regulation X (12 CFR 1024.17 and 1024.34).

rubrics_metrics.name: OCC factors for determining whether an activity is part of the business of banking
rubrics_metrics.description: The OCC considers: (i) whether the activity is the functional equivalent to, or a logical outgrowth of, a recognized banking activity; (ii) whether the activity strengthens the bank by benefiting its customers or its business; (iii) whether the activity involves risks similar in nature to those already assumed by banks; and (iv) whether the activity is authorized for State-chartered banks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The weight accorded to each factor depends on the facts and circumstances of each case; related incidental-activity factors consider whether the activity facilitates production or delivery of bank products/services or enables use of bank capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe-and-sound banking principles and contract compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks' real estate lending operations (including escrow operations) must be conducted pursuant to safe and sound banking principles and the terms of any applicable agreement with the borrower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where federal law vests broad discretion, activities should not contravene safety-and-soundness norms or contractual obligations; courts and OCC precedent frame this constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-law requirements may impose escrow compensation obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states require state-chartered banks to pay specified interest amounts on mortgage escrow accounts (examples listed include California, Connecticut, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Utah, Vermont, Wisconsin, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal flexibility does not override state statutes that require interest or other compensation; banks must comply with applicable state law in addition to federal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) requirement for information collections
rubrics_metrics.description: No agency may conduct or sponsor, nor is the respondent required to respond to, an information collection unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OCC reviewed the proposed rule and determined it does not create or revise any information collections, so no PRA submissions to OMB are required for this rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) / Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When required, an IRFA must contain: (1) a description of reasons why action is being considered; (2) a succinct statement of objectives of and legal basis for the proposed rule; (3) a description of and estimate of the number of small entities to which the rule will apply; (4) a description of projected reporting, recordkeeping, and other compliance requirements and an estimate of classes of small entities affected and professional skills necessary; (5) identification of relevant Federal rules that may duplicate, overlap, or conflict; and (6) a description of significant alternatives that accomplish the objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OCC's thresholds: it generally considers the economic impact on an individual small entity significant if >5% of total annual salaries and benefits or >2.5% of total non-interest expense; it considers 'substantial number' to be 5% or more of OCC-supervised small entities (approx. 30 entities). The OCC certified this proposed rule would not have significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it imposes no new direct costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) threshold and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: UMRA requires analysis where a Federal mandate may result in expenditures by governments or the private sector of $100 million or more in any one year (adjusted amount noted as $187 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proposed rule meets the UMRA threshold, the agency must prepare a written statement including a cost-benefit analysis. The OCC concluded the proposed rule imposes no new mandates and does not meet the UMRA threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12866 — significant regulatory action criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 12866 defines a 'significant regulatory action' as one likely to (1) have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or adversely affect economy/productivity/competition/jobs/environment/public health or safety, (2) create a serious inconsistency with another agency, (3) materially alter budgetary impacts of entitlements/grants/user fees/loan programs, or (4) raise novel legal or policy issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant actions require OIRA review and a cost-benefit analysis. The OCC reports OIRA determined this proposed rule is not a significant regulatory action under EO 12866.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 14192 — deregulatory offset requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 14192 requires an agency to identify at least 10 existing regulations to be repealed when the agency publicly proposes a new regulation with total costs greater than zero, and to offset new incremental costs by eliminating existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OCC states this proposed rule is deregulatory because it provides legal clarity that may reduce legal-related costs by clarifying banks' flexibility to structure escrow financing and compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific proposed amendments to 12 CFR parts 34 and 160
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed additions include: (a) adding a definition of 'Escrow account' to §34.2 (new paragraph (b)); (b) adding §34.3(d) stating national banks may establish or maintain escrow accounts and that terms/conditions (investment, fees, interest/compensation) are bank business decisions; (c) adding a definition of 'Escrow account' to §160.3 and adding §160.30(b) to permit Federal savings associations to establish or maintain escrow accounts with terms/conditions as business decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Register text provides the exact proposed regulatory wording to be inserted in parts 34 and 160; this is the operative regulatory change the OCC is proposing to codify existing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment submission and procedural instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments must be received on or before January 29, 2026. Commenters are encouraged to submit comments through the Federal eRulemaking Portal (Regulations.gov) using Docket ID 'OCC-2025-0736' and the title 'Real Estate Lending Escrow Accounts'; mail or hand-delivery options provided for Chief Counsel's Office with required agency and docket identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For help with submitting effective comments, use 'Commenter's Checklist' on Regulations.gov or call/email the helpdesk; contact numbers for OCC counsel are provided; the docket will be viewable after the close of comment period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment disclosure and confidentiality warning
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, the OCC will enter all comments received into the docket and publish the comments on the Regulations.gov website without change, including any business or personal information provided such as name and address information, email addresses, or phone numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may redact or withhold certain submissions (or portions) at their discretion; commenters are warned not to include information they consider confidential or inappropriate for public disclosure.
